fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "From News Arrows to the Smart Money World", "body": "Sterling traces his interest back to watching the up and down arrows on the news as a child, and to the 2008 crisis, which hit his father's work in the trades. The film The Big Short, about Michael Burry, showed him that traders could make money on markets going down as well as up. He says he began taking it seriously in 2019 after noticing hundreds of CEOs resign that fall, which he read as the sign of a coming black swan, then learned from mentors who had worked at pension funds, investment banks and hedge funds before trading his own capital."}, {"title": "Saturn, Mercury and the Alchemy of Time", "body": "Garton builds the episode's central image from a medieval alchemical engraving of Cronos, or Saturn, cutting Mercury off at the knees, and from Tracey Twyman's book Money Grows on the Tree of Knowledge, which argues that money only appears to be created ex nihilo and is really drawn from something intangible, time and human labor measured over time. Sterling supplies the modern figure on his slide: at a US average wage near thirty dollars an hour it now takes roughly 187 hours of work to buy one share of the S&P 500, against ten to twenty hours fifty years ago."}, {"title": "Money Velocity and the Speeding Up of Life", "body": "Sterling's slides argue that a thirty year mortgage has buyers paying for more than two houses once interest is counted, and that a 401k or IRA leaves a person long only and exposed to events like the 2020 crash. Garton reads Twyman on fractional reserve lending and money velocity, where a recession is a lack of velocity rather than simply a lack of money, and where inflating the supply while wages stay pegged to time means working longer for the same value as youth drains away. Garton calls the constant recession talk part of the spell."}, {"title": "Pump and Dumps and the Trader as Sacrifice", "body": "Sterling calls himself probably the world's biggest hater of crypto, describing Bitcoin as pure speculation with nothing backing it and the wave of celebrity coins as pump and dumps in the mold of Beanie Babies. He argues day trading works the same way, with online gurus telling followers to copy their trades and using them as liquidity to get out, and citing a Berkeley study he says ninety percent of day traders lose ninety percent of their money within ninety days. Garton reads Twyman on mortgage as death pledge and bond as bondage, calling the churn a sacrificial machine."}, {"title": "Temple Coins, Put Options and Chosen Sacrifice", "body": "Garton traces hedging back to Juno Moneta, the Roman goddess of memory and warning whose temple housed the mint, arguing that every coin was a receipt for a sacrifice and a hedge against divine wrath, and that where the ancients offered goats, wheat and incense, the modern trader offers a put option. Sterling defines a hedge as a trade made to reduce the risk of an adverse price move, answers Garton's ethics question by calling trading amoral because money and the corporate charter are artificial, and says he uses panicked headlines as liquidity to exit his positions."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Brandon Sterling joins InnerVerse to discuss how strategic trading reflects the process of alchemy, supported by Chance's analysis of Money Grows on the Tree of Knowledge by Tracy Twyman. We explore the mirror of modern markets and ancient temple rituals, how your time is being transmuted into someone else’s gold, and how to take your spiritual currency back and generate your own wealth.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: From insider insights to market metaphysics, this is more than a money talk; it's a revelation of financial sorcery and a launch pad to monetary sovereignty. Learn how Brandon’s Trading Business Builders course can guide you to reclaim your time and value from the economic matrix.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Trading as Modern Ritual Sacrifice", "body": "Chance traces the word shekel back to a bushel of wheat exchanged at the temple for a coin, and reframes those ancient temple coins as something like casino chips: proof of a sacrifice made, redeemable not for goods but for divination, a blessing from the priest, or a healing ritual. He argues the modern options trader performs the same structured offering to the unknown, risking real money the way ancient supplicants risked theirs, calling it functionally a prayer to God for a specific blessing. Brandon extends the metaphor, calling the whole system a philosopher's stone: a repeatable method for transmuting time and effort into refined value through volatility."}, {"title": "The Macro to Micro Forecasting Pyramid", "body": "Brandon lays out what he calls the macro to micro pyramid: GDP sits at the top, feeding down through industries like agriculture and retail into individual companies. He names forecasting tools traders rely on, including macro whispers about headwinds and tailwinds, distinct from the rear view mirror of a stock chart retail traders mistake for a forecasting tool. This sets up his thesis, borrowed from trader Jesse Livermore's line about the right side of the market: rather than betting purely bullish or bearish, his system stays directionally agnostic, holding long and short positions so one wrong call can't wipe out the account."}, {"title": "Why Hedge Funds Split Their Bets", "body": "Brandon explains hedge funds get their name from running a long short portfolio, roughly half the positions betting an asset falls and half betting it rises, so a wrong call on overall market direction doesn't take the whole fund out. He distinguishes contrarian short sellers like Michael Burry from activist short sellers, who publicize a company's wrongdoing and profit as the stock drops, citing the real case of electric vehicle company Nikola being exposed for faking a working semi truck. He frames shorting as a market function that keeps companies honest, since a company caught lying gets punished in price the way it wouldn't in less transparent markets."}, {"title": "The Philosopher's Stone of Risk-Adjusted Return", "body": "Chance calls the trading system itself a philosopher's stone, not a literal rock but a repeatable method for turning time and effort into refined value through volatility. Brandon grounds this in risk-adjusted return: an S&P 500 gain of 25% in a year actually carries an analyzed risk closer to 28%, because of black swan sized drawdowns like Covid baked into any asset class. He insists there's no shortcut playbook to hand over, since every trade is treated as a hypothesis the trader could be entirely wrong about, with the reward sized to pay out past a hundred percent when they're right."}, {"title": "How Options Actually Work", "body": "Brandon breaks down options through a property analogy: paying a small fee to lock in the right, not the obligation, to buy an asset at a set price before a deadline, then either exercising it or selling the contract itself for a profit. He contrasts options with futures, noting options reach thousands of assets versus a dozen or so macro products, and don't require the leverage that can wipe out an account if a large, over-allocated trade moves against you. He also walks through options spreads, pairing a long call with a short call at a higher strike to cap losses."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "The whole point of my system is to be directionally agnostic, not just bullish or bearish.", "author": "Brandon Sterling", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e699d708-52c0-482d-8d12-e02479d4ee12/BRANDON-STERLING.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "If you're just one side of this equation, if you're just bull, you're going to create the conditions for bear, for yourself.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The adept trader is a true alchemist because he is no longer reacting to the swings of fear and greed, of up and down, of gain and loss.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Shorting and ethics do go together, because shorting is a market function. It actually does keep companies in check.", "author": "Brandon Sterling", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e699d708-52c0-482d-8d12-e02479d4ee12/BRANDON-STERLING.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The philosopher stone isn't a rock, it's a system in trading, a repeatable method for taking the base of time and effort and transmuting it using volatility.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "People often ask me, Brandon, I need the exact trading rules playbook, gimme that, I need the book on it. And it's like, it doesn't exist.", "author": "Brandon Sterling", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e699d708-52c0-482d-8d12-e02479d4ee12/BRANDON-STERLING.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The guy glued on the screen trading stock, like actual stocks, waking up at market open 9:30 AM and searching for stocks. But that's not actually how those guys do it.", "author": "Brandon Sterling", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e699d708-52c0-482d-8d12-e02479d4ee12/BRANDON-STERLING.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You doing the options trading is you're making the prayer to God, you're making this application, you are making the plea or the intention to the divine.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You could lose your whole account very easily, if not more, because you're trading with more cash than you actually have.", "author": "Brandon Sterling", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e699d708-52c0-482d-8d12-e02479d4ee12/BRANDON-STERLING.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "In the risk assessment, we are willing to admit we could be a hundred percent wrong. However, in the reward aspect of that ratio, it can go past a hundred percent.", "author": "Brandon Sterling", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e699d708-52c0-482d-8d12-e02479d4ee12/BRANDON-STERLING.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
